characters: Ohenewaa: a sweet six-year-old Ghanaian girl with two neat braided puffs, wearing a lavender-and-yellow school dress by day and soft yellow pyjamas at bedtime.
Mama: her caring Ghanaian mother wearing an indigo-and-gold African-print wrapper cloth and matching headwrap.
Madam Salamatu: her gentle class teacher in a bright emerald-and-gold patterned dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A yawning, grumpy voice at first for Ohenewaa; a bright voice at the end; a kind voice for Mama and Madam Salamatu
narrationPlan.pace: Heavy and yawning at the start, bright at the end (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A slow, sleepy lullaby tune that brightens in the morning (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Many Ghanaian households share evening routines together; the story models gentle adult guidance without shaming a tired child.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (via CDC Healthy Schools) recommends 9–12 hours of sleep per 24 hours for children aged 6–12 (and 10–13 hours including naps for ages 3–5), along with consistent bedtimes and turning screens off before bed.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Verify that the 9–12 hours sleep guidance for school-age children (6–12 years) aligns with health guidance.
Confirm that the tone remains warm and supportive for families sharing sleeping spaces.

teacherGuide.overview: A warm, relatable story for young learners showing how enough sleep supports memory, growth, and kindness, and modelling a simple screen-free bedtime routine.
learningGoals: Give three reasons why sleep is important.
Order four steps of a healthy bedtime routine.
Choose one calm habit to practise before bed tonight.
beforeReading: Ask: how does your body feel in the morning when you go to bed early versus very late?
whileReading: Let learners stretch and pretend to yawn on page 1, then sit tall and smile brightly on page 5.
afterReading: Draw four small pictures showing your own evening bedtime routine.
Share your favourite bedtime story or lullaby from home.
discussion: Why was Ohenewaa cross with her friend on page 2?
How did switching screens off early help her?
reflection: What is one calm thing you can do before bed tonight?

support: Sequence four picture cards: supper, toothbrushing, story, sleep.
stretch: Tell a younger sibling or cousin three reasons why our brains love sleep.

culturalNotes: Many Ghanaian households share evening routines together; the story models gentle adult guidance without shaming a tired child.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (via CDC Healthy Schools) recommends 9–12 hours of sleep per 24 hours for children aged 6–12 (and 10–13 hours including naps for ages 3–5), along with consistent bedtimes and turning screens off before bed.
localiseThis: Include familiar evening habits such as bathing with warm water, family prayers or songs, and oral stories.
Be sensitive to children who share rooms and do not set household light times alone.

factCheck.claim: School-age children aged 6–12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep per night.
factCheck.explanation: Adequate nightly sleep supports physical growth, emotional regulation, attention, and memory consolidation in school-age learners.
factCheck.reference: American Academy of Sleep Medicine / CDC Healthy Schools Sleep Guidelines (ages 6–12: 9–12 hours; ages 3–5: 10–13 hours)
